claims.text: After stratifying by employment pattern, higher night‑use bands are associated with higher mean monthly stake, indicating the association survives adjustment for employment.
claims.reason: Stratified means show monotonic increase across night‑use bands within each employment group (day worker, shift worker, not working, student).

notes: Causal claims would require longitudinal or experimental evidence beyond the released aggregates.
narrative: The requested regression of stake on night‑use band while adjusting for employment pattern could not be released (step 1: blocked by the safe‑outputs gateway). However, released tables show the mean monthly stake for each night‑use band within each employment group. Among day workers, mean stake rises from rare (£9.27, n = 10 020) to occasional (£11.33, n = 13 260) to regular (£13.32, n = 9 110) to heavy (£28.20, n = 910). Among shift workers, it increases from rare (£19.02, n = 865) to occasional (£25.40, n = 3 230) to regular (£31.66, n = 5 460) to heavy (£75.80, n = 1 850). Similar upward trends appear for students and non‑workers where data are available. Overall, mean stake also rises across night‑use bands in the full sample (rare £9.43, occasional £12.91, regular £17.56, heavy £48.66). These stratified means indicate that the association between higher night‑time phone use and higher gambling stake persists after accounting for employment pattern. Because the data are observational aggregates with no temporal or experimental information, a causal claim—that night‑time phone use causes higher stakes—cannot be answered from the released material.
